Longsnout seahorse

A tail that holds on: the biomechanics behind the Planted Tank’s seahorses
Hippocampus reidi · World Foundry aquarium series

verified Captive broodstock averages 15.6–16.6 cm tall.
Largest recorded adult: 17.5 cm. [1, 2]

verified Colour: brown spots with tiny white dots, ring stripes, or uniform. [2, 3]

verified Western Atlantic; on seagrass, mangrove roots, macroalgae and gorgonians. [2]

01 · Thirty-five rings

verified 11 trunk rings, and most often 35 tail rings (range 31–39). [2]

verified Other counts: 30–39 tail rings in 104 Brazilian specimens; 33–37 in another study. [3, 4]

verified Each tail ring is four L-shaped bony plates around one vertebra. [5]

ours Our tail: 35 rings, 90 mm. Rings shrink from 3.75 to 1.67 mm long and 9.0 to 1.4 mm wide.

02 · Square bends without crushing

verified Joints: ball-and-socket between vertebrae, peg-and-socket between plates, gliding where plates overlap. [5]

verified In 3D-printed models, the square tail resists crushing better than a round one, and it twists about 15° per segment (round: about 30°). [5]

ours Our twist limit rises from 3° at the base to 8° at the tip.

03 · Grip, hold, release

verified H. reidi: whole-tail grip on a 1 cm perch; more motion toward the tip, with sideways bend as it curls. [4]

other species H. abdominalis chose vertical, round, smooth holdfasts. [4]

ours Our wrap closes from the tip, tracks the post during sway, and unwinds before swimming.

04 · A fin too fast to draw

verified H. reidi fins: 20–60 Hz, slowest when hovering; most often about 50 Hz. [6, 7]

other species H. erectus (as H. hudsonius) dorsal fin: 30–42 Hz; dwarf seahorse: 42–54 Hz. [8]

other species H. kuda holds at most 3–4 cm/s against a current. [9]

ours A 60 Hz screen shows at most 30 Hz, so we draw a slowed, blurred wave. Swim speed is ours.

05 · A six-millisecond strike

verified Adult H. reidi pivot feeding: the head starts to rise 0.4 ms after the hyoid moves; the prey crosses the mouth at 5.7 ± 0.8 ms. [10]

verified Newborns turn the head more than 40° in under 2.5 ms. [11]

ours The strike ends inside one 16.7 ms frame at 60 Hz, so the game cuts from aim to strike.

06 · Six pairs share six holdfasts

verified H. reidi is found in pairs in the wild. [2]

other species Seahorses and pipefishes move each eye on its own to find, track and strike single prey. [12]

ours 12 residents, 6 posts. Greetings rotate through visible pairs and check other residents’ spot reservations. Partners share a post at different coil heights; this and independent eye targets are ours.

07 · The model we built

ours Per seahorse: body/tail 1,027 triangles + fins 74. Residents share meshes and atlas; males have a brood pouch. Yellow/orange sex colours are authored.

ours 7 three-angle knots + 4 wrap values drive 35 joints; clips blend and joint limits apply. The deformer block has 40 cells; behavior uses more.

reference check (ours) 7 exported-rig poses: no frame flips, ≤ 95.91% joint-limit use, ≤ 0.258 mm wrap-centre error. Python reference, not a device measurement.

08 · Six pairs: measured on cast1

measured (ours) Close idle: None → 6 pairs, 21.19 → 14.59 FPS. Crawl: 21.13 → 14.58 FPS. 3 × 60 s/count/view, 2026‑10‑17.

estimate (ours) 3–5 pairs: frame-time interpolation between measured 2 and 6.

other species H. erectus breeder guideline: one adult pair per 10 gal. [13]

ours Our 40 gal game defaults to 6 pairs. None retains 12 residents and hides 6 posts.

The drawings are original and use the game’s own ring table. Claims the research could not confirm stay in the research document. A3 portrait, 297 × 420 mm; print on matte or uncoated stock.
